study_identification_part.si4_title: Brain morphology normative modelling platform for abnormality and centile estimation: Brain MoNoCle

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop and validate Brain MoNoCle, an accessible web-based normative modeling platform for brain morphology analysis that combines multiple key features (user-friendly interface, individual and group outputs, multi-site analysis, regional and whole-brain analysis, integration with existing tools, and multiple morphology metrics) in one open-source application.

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Statistical outlier detection: residuals >5 median absolute deviations from gamlss model flagged as outliers; visual inspection of plots for each dataset (brain metrics vs age at hemisphere level); cross-checking of statistical and visual outliers; listwise deletion of participants flagged as outliers in any model to ensure same normative reference dataset across all models; some public datasets included QC as part of original study design (reported in original publications)
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: Some of the public datasets included quality control steps as part of the study design, which are reported in the original study publications. We detected outliers in the entire dataset statistically: we ran our gamlss model described below for each structural metric for each region, and flagged outliers defined by residuals more than five median absolute deviations. In addition, we also detected outliers based on visual inspections of plots: for each dataset, we plotted each brain metric at the hemisphere level against age to flag outliers within each dataset. These were then cross checked with outliers that were detected statistically. We excluded participants who were flagged as an outlier in any of these models; we performed listwise deletion rather than pairwise deletion so that the same normative reference dataset was used for each normative model, allowing comparisons of model statistics across models.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: GAMLSS with site as random effect for mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ); site effects modeled hierarchically; age (smooth function), sex (fixed effect), and site (random effect) included in model; harmonization integrated into normative model rather than separate preprocessing step (e.g., Combat); avoids separate Combat-style assumptions of normality; for unseen sites, site-specific mean estimated from ≥10 healthy controls and site-specific variance estimated from ≥30 healthy controls; if <30 controls, average standard deviation across normative sites used instead; residuals calculated relative to reference normative site then adjusted for new site offset
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: Generalized additive models for location scale and shape (GAMLSS) using the gamlss package were used to simultaneously model the parameters (mean, standard deviation, skew, and kurtosis) of the distribution as response variables of the explanatory variables sex, age, and scanning site/batch. Specifically, in our model, the mean depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age; the standard deviation depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age... For example, our model harmonises scanning site effects for mean and variance, avoiding separate steps as found in Combat (Johnson et al., 2007), which makes separate assumptions. Specifically, Combat assumes that after removing covariate effects on the mean, the data are normally distributed, and site effects on mean and variance are estimated based on this assumption. However, this is often not the case... First, we predicted the distribution parameters based on the HCs in each new site/batch and calculated residuals relative to one of the normative scanning sites. The mean of the residuals from the HCs in the unseen data was then used to calculate the site-specific offset needed to harmonise the unseen dataset with the normative data... if there are less than 30 HCs, we used the average standard deviation seen across normative data sites/batches... We estimated the standard deviation from the unseen HCs only if there were 30 or more HCs in the dataset.

nm2_modeling_method.supporting_text: Generalized additive models for location scale and shape (GAMLSS) using the gamlss package (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/gamlss/) were used to simultaneously model the parameters (mean, standard deviation, skew, and kurtosis) of the distribution as response variables of the explanatory variables sex, age, and scanning site/batch. Specifically, in our model, the mean depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age; the standard deviation depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age; the skew depends on sex (fixed effect) and a smooth function of age; and the kurtosis depends on a smooth function of age... nm9_nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The paper describes a proper held-out independent validation approach in the subsampling stability analysis (Supplementary S3). They held out 200 subjects randomly sampled across sites to serve as a test set, then trained normative models on varying subsample sizes (excluding the 200 held-out subjects), and assessed model performance on these truly held-out 200 subjects. Performance metrics include: (1) Pearson correlation coefficient between residuals from subsampled models vs. full model; (2) Mean absolute error (MAE) of predictions. The key point is that the 200 held-out subjects were excluded from all model training (both subsampled and full models were trained on n=3,076, excluding the 200), making this a proper independent same-domain validation with normative parameters re-estimated on training data only.

caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper describes multiple deviation metrics used throughout the analyses. Z-scores are the primary individual-level metric, calculated through a multi-step process described in detail. Centiles are calculated as an alternative metric using the full distribution parameters. For group comparisons, Cohen's d effect sizes are reported. The threshold for extreme/abnormal deviations is explicitly mentioned as 2 standard deviations (|z|≥2). For lateralization analysis in epilepsy, the difference between left and right hemisphere z-scores is used, with performance evaluated via confusion matrices and accuracy metrics. Total outlier count and proportion of extreme deviations are also used as summary metrics.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-level comparisons using Cohen's d effect sizes for BD and mTLE cohorts comparing clinical groups to normative distribution; Pearson correlation analysis comparing Brain MoNoCle effect sizes with ENIGMA study effect sizes for external validation (r>0.5 for mTLE); Cross-platform comparison: correlation of z-scores between Brain MoNoCle and CentileBrain (correlation >0.75 in ~80% of regions); Individual-level lateralization prediction using sign of hemispheric z-score difference (left - right); Performance metrics: confusion matrices, accuracy (>0.75 for volume and I), sensitivity/specificity for lateralization; Proportion of patients with extreme deviations (|z|>2) calculated and reported as percentages; Visual inspection via violin plots showing distribution of z-score differences by group (controls, left mTLE, right mTLE); Comparison of traditional case-control approach vs normative modeling approach for BD cohort to demonstrate superiority of normative framework
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Brain MoNoCle successfully replicated ENIGMA findings in bipolar disorder and temporal lobe epilepsy using normative modeling with small clinical samples; individual-level abnormalities in cortical volume and isometric size (I) showed strong agreement with seizure lateralization (>75% accuracy); the novel independent morphometric K showed superior normative model fit (R²=0.8) compared to traditional metrics (R²=0.4-0.6), suggesting it better captures biological covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Validation in bipolar disorder (n=56) demonstrated that normative modeling yielded abnormality estimates more consistent with large-scale ENIGMA findings than traditional case-control comparison using matched controls (n=26). Specifically, normative modeling revealed cortical thinning in left pre-central gyrus (Cohen's d=-0.8) consistent with ENIGMA, whereas case-control comparison showed thickening (d=0.70), illustrating superiority of normative approach. In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (n=133 mTLE; 99 HC), group-level cortical thickness abnormalities showed widespread thinning especially in right mTLE affecting precentral gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and inferior parietal gyrus, with Pearson correlation >0.5 between Brain MoNoCle effect sizes and ENIGMA-epilepsy study findings, confirming reproducibility. Individual-level validation demonstrated that cortical volume and isometric size component (I) best captured seizure lateralization: 78.2% of patients showed correct laterality for cortical volume (36.1% outside 2 SD), and 75.9% for I metric (32.3% outside 2 SD), with overall lateralization accuracy >0.75 for both metrics; in contrast, traditional cortical thickness showed poor lateralization. Cross-metric comparison revealed that independent component K exhibited markedly superior normative model fit (R²=0.8 for both hemispheres) compared to all traditional metrics including cortical thickness, volume, and surface area (R²=0.4-0.6), indicating biological covariates (age, sex, site) are substantially better explained by K metric, which showed steeper declines in early and later life. Cross-platform validation with CentileBrain showed good agreement (correlation >0.75 in approximately 80% of brain regions). Model stability analysis confirmed convergence at sample sizes ≥2000 subjects with >99.5% correlation between subset-trained and full models.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited to cortical morphology, not subcortical structures which are particularly relevant for mTLE (hippocampal changes); number of sites (21) is at lower boundary for optimal random effects modeling (recommended >20); current normative sample lacks diverse global geographical representation; vertex-wise analysis not yet implemented; single parcellation scheme (Desikan-Killiany, 68 regions) currently available; longitudinal data modeling not yet implemented; requires healthy control data from new sites (minimum n=10 for mean, n=30 for variance estimation)

We included 21 sites, and suggest that future work should prioritize increasing the number of sites in normative datasets, with diverse global representation, rather than focusing solely on total subject count. ... clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Platform implements novel calibration approach for new unseen sites requiring local healthy controls (minimum n=10 for mean estimation, n=30 for variance estimation; if <30 controls, average SD across normative sites used instead); offers unified framework for exploring multiple morphology metrics enabling direct comparison of traditional (thickness, volume, surface area) and novel independent components (K, I, S) under same statistical model; freely accessible as web-based tool at https://cnnplab.shinyapps.io/BrainMoNoCle/ requiring no coding or software installation; accepts direct FreeSurfer outputs (aparcstats2table csv files) and Cortical Folding toolbox outputs; exports include individual z-scores and centiles (csv files), group summary statistics, brain visualization plots, scatter plots, and comprehensive HTML reports; site harmonization integrated into distributional modeling avoiding separate Combat-style preprocessing and its normality assumptions; sinh-arcsinh distribution allows flexible non-Gaussian modeling of skew and kurtosis; model stability confirmed via subsampling analysis showing convergence at n≈2000; platform enables both hypothesis-driven analyses (specific clinical groups) and exploratory metric comparisons to identify which morphological measures best capture disease effects

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study presents Brain MoNoCle (Brain Morphology Normative modelling platform for abnormality and Centile estimation), an open-source web-based platform combining six key features for brain morphology normative modeling in one unified application. Complete normative dataset details in Supplementary Table S1.1: 21 sites across 13 datasets - ADHD1000 (n=153), BLISS (n=26), CamCAN sites 1&2 (n=495+83), Chronotype (n=126), Greene-HM (n=22), HCP (n=678), MEGUK sites Aston1/Aston2/Cambridge/Glasgow/Oxford (n=29+69+71+24+63), NCL-dementia sites 1&2 (n=29+26), NIMH-IHV sites 1&2 (n=48+54), NKI (n=790), OASIS3 (n=355), Stanford-CR (n=40), UCLH sites 1&3 (n=28+67); total N=3,276, age 5-95 years (median 33), 58.3% female. FreeSurfer versions varied: 5.2 (HCP), 5.3.0 (CamCAN), 6.0.1 (BLISS, NCL-dementia, NKI), 7.3.2 (all others). Platform introduces novel independent morphometric components (K, I, S) based on universal scaling law of cortical folding (Mota & Herculano-Houzel, 2015; Wang et al., 2016, 2019, 2021) alongside traditional FreeSurfer metrics. Model formula comparison via weighted AIC across 11 alternative GAMLSS specifications confirmed chosen model (Model 1: μ~sex+site+s(age); σ~sex+site+s(age); ν~sex+s(age); τ~s(age)) was optimal or near-optimal across most regions and metrics, though Model 6 adding site random effect to skew showed better fit in some regions but was not implemented to maintain consistency and enable application to small new-site samples. Calibration data: IDEAS HC (n=99) and BLISS HC (n=26) used for site-specific offset and variance estimation when applying normative model to clinical cohorts. Planned future developments: multiscale morphometrics, additional parcellation atlases (beyond Desikan-Killiany), vertex-wise analysis, longitudinal modeling with within-subject correlations, subcortical volumes, integration with CIVET and volBrain outputs. Key methodological innovation: integrated site harmonization within distributional model (GAMLSS with random effects) avoiding Combat's separate preprocessing step and normality assumptions, instead using flexible sinh-arcsinh distribution allowing all four moments to vary with covariates. Platform enables both replication of established findings (ENIGMA validation) and novel discoveries (K metric's superior covariate capture, volume/I metrics' superiority for epilepsy lateralization).
